context: Fiona has a collection of discs labelled with the consecutive whole numbers from 1 up to the total number of discs. One disc is selected at random, and we want the probability that its number is a multiple of two given numbers at once.

params.name: a
params.choice: [d for d in range(2, b) if b % d == 0]

params.require: (rem != 0 and rem * 10 < 4 * total) or rem * 10 > 6 * total
params.why: the exact probability is never an exact two-decimal value and never close to a rounding boundary, so rounding is unambiguous

stem: Fiona has ${=total}$ labelled discs, which are numbered from $1$ to ${=total}$. If a disc is selected at random, what is the probability that the disc number is a multiple of both ${=a}$ and ${=b}$? Give your answer as a decimal number, rounded to two decimal places.
solution: A disc that is a multiple of ${=a}$ and of ${=b}$ lies in both events. Let $A$ be the event 'a multiple of ${=a}$' and $B$ the event 'a multiple of ${=b}$'. We need $P(A\cap B)$.
Since ${=b}={=a}\times{=b // a}$, every multiple of ${=b}$ is also a multiple of ${=a}$.
So the set of discs that are multiples of both ${=a}$ and ${=b}$ is the same as the set of multiples of ${=b}$: ${=b}$, ${=2 * b}$, ${=3 * b}$, $\ldots$
The largest multiple of ${=b}$ that is not more than ${=total}$ is ${=cnt}\times{=b}={=cnt * b}$ (the next one, ${=(cnt + 1) * b}$, is more than ${=total}$), so $n(A\cap B)={=cnt}$.
The sample space has $n(S)={=total}$ discs, so $P(A\cap B)=\frac{n(A\cap B)}{n(S)}=\frac{{=cnt}}{{=total}}$.
Therefore, the probability that the disc number is a multiple of both ${=a}$ and ${=b}$ is ${=ans}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Uses the product of the two numbers
proposed_misconceptions.description: Treats 'a multiple of a and of b' as 'a multiple of a×b' and counts multiples of that product, even though b is already a multiple of a so the multiples of b are exactly the discs wanted.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Counts the multiples of the smaller number only
proposed_misconceptions.description: Counts the discs that are multiples of a (the smaller number) and treats them as the intersection, forgetting that the disc must also be a multiple of b.

notes: Advanced: the book's own twist from ex14-8-13g (page 493): when a divides b, 'a multiple of a and of b' is just 'a multiple of b', so the learner must see the intersection without being given the event sets, count it, divide by n(S) and round. b is composite (4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15) and a is a divisor of b strictly between 1 and b (the lcm is never needed, which the book does not use). Sample space 60 to 120 discs so there are always at least 3 multiples of b (k >= 4 in practice). The require makes the exact value a non-terminating-at-2dp number whose fractional part at the hundredths place lies in (0, 0.4) or (0.6, 1), so '\approx' is always honest and a solver rounding a 4-decimal intermediate gets the same answer. Checked by brute force: for all 639 admissible (a, b, total) combinations the count of discs divisible by both equals total // b, and the two-decimal answer is the same whether rounded from the exact fraction or from a four-decimal value.
